---
name: statement-vacuity-vs-proof-vacuity
description: Passing the "does the statement mention its object" check is what stops you asking whether the PROOF uses it; understating generality fails to foreclose a route
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

I audited my own refutation against this round's stated bar — never write a declaration whose
statement does not mention the object it is about (the `HasDivFunctor` test) — and passed
honestly. Every declaration named `pic0SigmaSheaf`, `restrictChart`, the real
`IsLocallySurjective` class. Then I wrote "no divisor data, no chart data, no `rep`" about the
proof and stopped. A fresh-context audit re-proved my theorem verbatim for an **arbitrary
presheaf of types on `Scheme`** — no `pic⁰`, no curve, no field, no sheaf condition — and derived
mine from it by defeq.

**Why:** the two checks measure opposite things. The statement check asks *is the object
present*; the proof check asks *is the object used*. A theorem can be honestly about `C` while
its proof is generic in `C` — and passing the first check supplies the feeling of having audited,
which is exactly what suppresses the second.

The cost is not untidiness. The narrow statement leaves open a question the general one closes:
could a `pic⁰`-side repair (different sheafification, different Σ-extension, finer site) evade the
refuted endpoint? Against a statement `pic⁰` does not occur in, no. So understating generality
**fails to foreclose a route** — the same cost as a false discount, arriving disguised as modesty.

**How to apply:** when a theorem lands, restate it with the geometry replaced by a variable of
the weakest type its proof touches, and retypecheck the *same* script. If it goes through, that
is where the theorem lives. Same move as [[delete-the-geometry-and-retypecheck]], but applied to
a theorem that already works rather than to a stuck residue. Related:
[[read-what-the-step-outputs]], [[generic-engines-vs-residue-carrier]].

---
name: a-control-that-cannot-fail-differently
description: "The identical script fails at the other endpoint" is a fact about a lemma name, not a measurement — the control you want is a theorem at that endpoint
metadata:

I refuted a coverage instance at `V = ⊥` and offered as evidence that the parameter mattered:
*re-running the identical proof script with `⊤` in place of `⊥` fails.* True, reproducible, and
worthless. The script fails at the application of `isEmpty_of_hom_bot` — a lemma that cannot apply
at `⊤` **by its own statement**, and would fail identically at *every* `V`, including any at
which the refutation genuinely holds.

**Why:** a control has to be something that could have come out the other way. Mine was a
tautology about a name. It reads like diligence in a report and passes every mechanical check,
because the failure is real — it just is not evidence of what I claimed.

The control I actually wanted was six lines away and already implied by the tree: a **theorem** at
the other endpoint (`at ⊤ the restricted atlas inherits coverage`), which says a `⊤` analogue of
my refutation would refute the project's own target. That is falsifiable, and it is what makes the
`⊥` result a statement about `⊥`.

**How to apply:** before writing "measured: X fails at the other end", ask what would have
happened if the endpoint did *not* matter. If the answer is "the same failure", the observation is
about a lemma's signature. Reach instead for a positive statement at that endpoint — often already
in the tree, since a project working toward a target has usually proved the good case somewhere.
